workloads.label: Short, bursty events
workloads.detail: Stateless handlers run briefly and demand can jump quickly.

workloads.label: Long-running API
workloads.detail: A continuously available service needs stable runtime and connection behavior.

workloads.label: Relational transactions
workloads.detail: Durable records, transactions, backups, and recovery are the primary contract.

workloads.label: Asynchronous batch
workloads.detail: Finite jobs favor queueing, throughput, retry control, and economical capacity.

latencies.label: Tight tail latency
latencies.detail: Startup and scheduling variance must stay off the critical path.

latencies.label: Interactive seconds
latencies.detail: Normal web or API latency with bounded autoscaling delay is acceptable.

latencies.label: Minutes are acceptable
latencies.detail: Queueing and startup delay matter less than throughput and cost.

operations.label: Low operations tolerance
operations.detail: The product team cannot own hosts, clusters, or database maintenance.

operations.label: Shared operations capacity
operations.detail: The team can own workload configuration and some platform controls.

operations.label: Dedicated platform capacity
operations.detail: Specialists can operate upgrades, policy, capacity, and recovery.

consistencies.label: Strict regional transactions
consistencies.detail: Committed reads and writes need conventional transaction semantics in one region.

consistencies.label: Strong multi-region reads
consistencies.detail: Globally placed clients need a documented strong-consistency contract.

consistencies.label: Eventual convergence
consistencies.detail: Temporary stale reads or asynchronous reconciliation are acceptable.

portabilities.label: Provider outcomes first
portabilities.detail: Managed productivity can outweigh migration effort.

portabilities.label: Balanced portability
portabilities.detail: Keep application boundaries portable while accepting selected managed services.

portabilities.label: Exit path is a priority
portabilities.detail: Runtime, data, and operations must move with bounded redesign.

categories.label: Event-driven functions
categories.fitReason: Burst scaling and event integration reduce idle platform work when each invocation is short and stateless.
categories.consistencyContract: The function runtime does not define data consistency; the backing store and application protocol do.
categories.failure: Cold starts, concurrency quotas, duplicate delivery, timeout limits, and downstream connection storms remain application concerns.
categories.verify: Measure startup percentiles, burst throttling, retry duplication, maximum duration, and downstream saturation.
categories.equivalenceCaveat: Trigger catalogs, concurrency controls, runtime limits, networking, and retry semantics differ.

categories.label: Managed container runtime
categories.fitReason: A container preserves runtime control while the provider owns most host placement, replacement, and scaling machinery.
categories.consistencyContract: A portable image does not provide a portable state contract; databases, queues, and identity still need separate decisions.
categories.failure: Startup delay, health checks, request draining, autoscaling limits, and connection exhaustion must be designed and tested.
categories.verify: Measure scale-from-zero, steady concurrency, private networking, rollout rollback, connection draining, and quota behavior.
categories.equivalenceCaveat: Scaling units, request limits, background work, networking, and deployment models are not identical.

providers.aws: Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate or AWS App Runner

categories.label: Managed Kubernetes
categories.role: Managed control plane with customer-operated workloads
categories.fitReason: Kubernetes is credible when scheduling, policy, sidecars, or a shared platform justify cluster lifecycle and on-call ownership.
categories.consistencyContract: Kubernetes standardizes workload orchestration, not the semantics or recovery of application data.
categories.failure: The team still owns nodes or profiles, upgrades, policies, workload health, autoscaling, stateful recovery, and platform incidents.
categories.verify: Test cluster and node upgrades, node loss, policy enforcement, autoscaling, workload disruption, and platform-team response.
categories.equivalenceCaveat: Node models, networking, identity, upgrade channels, add-ons, and control-plane integrations differ.

categories.label: Virtual machines
categories.fitReason: Virtual machines are credible when host agents, unsupported runtimes, licensing, or specialized networking outweigh lifecycle work.
categories.consistencyContract: Host control does not create durable consistency; state ownership and replication remain separate architecture choices.
categories.failure: The team owns image hygiene, operating-system patches, process recovery, replacement, autoscaling, and host observability.
categories.verify: Test immutable image builds, patch rollout, host replacement, autoscaling, backup restore, and zonal loss.
categories.equivalenceCaveat: Machine families, disks, live maintenance, networking, licensing, and discount models differ.

categories.label: Managed batch scheduler
categories.role: Queued finite jobs on managed capacity
categories.fitReason: A batch scheduler makes queueing, retries, parallelism, and finite job completion explicit without running a general platform.
categories.consistencyContract: Input snapshots, output commits, idempotency, and replay determine consistency across batch attempts.
categories.failure: Partial output, repeated jobs, queue starvation, quota pressure, and non-idempotent retries can corrupt results or extend completion time.
categories.verify: Test retry isolation, checkpointing, cancellation, quota exhaustion, spot interruption, and partial-output cleanup.
categories.equivalenceCaveat: Queue semantics, supported capacity, scheduling policy, data locality, and interruption behavior differ.

categories.label: Managed regional relational database
categories.role: Conventional transactions with managed engine operations
categories.fitReason: A managed relational service is the default starting point for regional transactions when the engine contract fits.
categories.consistencyContract: Primary-region transactions can be strict while replicas, failover, and cross-region reads have separate lag and promotion semantics.
categories.failure: Connection limits, failover pauses, replica lag, maintenance, schema changes, and restore procedures still reach the application.
categories.verify: Measure transaction latency, failover interruption, replica lag, connection recovery, backup restore, and export duration.
categories.equivalenceCaveat: Engine choices, failover, replicas, extensions, maintenance, backup, and network contracts differ.

providers.gcp: Cloud SQL or AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
providers.azure: Azure SQL Database or Azure Database for PostgreSQL

categories.label: Distributed relational database
categories.fitReason: Distributed relational products are credible when multi-region consistency or horizontal scale is a measured requirement, not a future guess.
categories.consistencyContract: Consensus and replica placement can provide strong semantics, but distance, quorum, and topology affect write latency and availability.
categories.failure: Quorum loss, hot keys, transaction contention, regional partitions, and schema or API differences can dominate behavior.
categories.verify: Benchmark the exact replica topology, cross-region writes, contention, partition behavior, recovery, and full data export.
categories.equivalenceCaveat: SQL compatibility, consistency controls, topology, transaction limits, and migration paths differ substantially.

providers.aws: No direct Cloud Spanner equivalent; investigate Aurora Global Database or an external distributed SQL product with different write semantics
providers.azure: No direct Cloud Spanner equivalent; investigate geo-replicated Azure SQL patterns or an external distributed SQL product

categories.label: Self-managed relational database
categories.fitReason: Self-management is credible only when required extensions, host control, or a tested exit path justify full database operations ownership.
categories.consistencyContract: The chosen engine defines local transactions; the team must design replication, fencing, promotion, backups, and recovery.
categories.failure: The team owns patching, backups, restore, replication, failover, capacity, corruption response, and every engine incident.
categories.verify: Rehearse patching, replica rebuild, leader fencing, backup restoration, point-in-time recovery, and complete regional loss.
categories.equivalenceCaveat: The database engine may be portable, but disks, networking, identity, automation, and operational tooling remain provider-specific.

providers.aws: PostgreSQL or MySQL on Amazon EC2
providers.gcp: PostgreSQL or MySQL on Compute Engine
providers.azure: PostgreSQL or MySQL on Azure Virtual Machines
